title: Indirect Command
subtitle: imperō / rogō ut + subjunctive.
objectives: Recognize indirect command with verbs of commanding/asking + ut/nē.
Translate as 'that', 'to', or infinitive in English.
Understand the difference between direct command (imperative) and indirect (ut + subj.).

sections.heading: Indirect command
sections.body:
Indirect commands follow verbs of commanding, asking, persuading, urging. They use ut + subjunctive (nē for negative).

rex imperāvit ut mīlitēs venīrent. — The king ordered that the soldiers come / ordered the soldiers to come.
tē rogō nē discēdās. — I ask you not to depart.

Common verbs: imperō, rogō, moneō, hortor, persuādeō, petō.

Caesar writes: legiōnibus imperāvit nē proelium committerent. — He ordered the legions not to engage in battle.

items.prompt: Translate: dux mīlitibus imperāvit ut fortiter pugnārent.
items.answer: The leader ordered the soldiers to fight bravely.
I warn you to be silent.

words.latin: Caesar legiōnibus imperāvit ut castra mūnīrent.
words.gloss: Caesar ordered the legions to fortify the camp.
